shared.concept_anchor: Article 31B Ninth Schedule — original intent vs post-IR Coelho review

en.display_text:
Assertion (a): Article 31B of the Constitution shields laws placed in the Ninth Schedule from being challenged on the ground of violating any of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Part III.

Reason (R): Following the Supreme Court's decision in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), laws that were inserted into the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 continue to enjoy absolute immunity from judicial review, including review on grounds of Fundamental Rights violations.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
en.strong_distractor: c — Option c (A correct but R incorrect) tempts students who believe IR Coelho made ALL Ninth Schedule laws reviewable, which would make R's claim about pre-1973 absolute immunity incorrect — but pre-1973 laws DO retain absolute immunity, making R correct.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (a) factually correct? — Yes. Article 31B grants laws placed in the Ninth Schedule immunity from challenge on grounds of violating Fundamental Rights — this is its stated function.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) factually correct? — Yes. After IR Coelho (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule BEFORE April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity — R is a correct and precise statement about the post-IR Coelho legal position.

Step 3: Does R causally or logically explain A? — Partially. R accurately describes the scope of 31B's immunity (what survived IR Coelho) but does not fully explain WHY 31B was created (which was to protect land reform laws from FR challenges). R explains the current limitation of 31B's immunity rather than its original rationale — the causal link between A's description of 31B's purpose and R's description of its post-IR Coelho scope is incomplete.
Both A and R are correct, but R describes the temporal limitation on 31B's immunity rather than causally explaining 31B's protective function — option b.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates in how R is constructed: it correctly describes that pre-1973 Ninth Schedule laws retain absolute immunity but adds 'this immunity was the original intent of Article 31B.' This conflates the original intent (protecting all Ninth Schedule laws from FR challenge) with what survived after IR Coelho (pre-1973 absolute immunity). R is factually correct as a statement about post-IR Coelho law but does not causally explain why Article 31B was inserted in 1951.
en.final_explanation:
Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule operate as a shield — but one that was reshaped by judicial review over six decades.

Assertion (a) analysis: Article 31B, inserted by the 1st Amendment (1951), declares that none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule shall be deemed void on the ground of being inconsistent with or taking away or abridging any of the rights conferred by Part III (Fundamental Rights). This accurately describes 31B's protective function.

Reason (R) analysis: After IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity from judicial review. This is a correct statement about the current legal position — Waman Rao (1981) and IR Coelho (2007) together create this temporal bifurcation.

Causal relationship: R is factually correct but describes a consequence of IR Coelho's ruling on 31B's scope — not the original rationale for 31B's insertion. The 1st Amendment created 31B to protect zamindari abolition laws from all FR challenges; the pre-1973 absolute immunity is what survived after IR Coelho's judicial recalibration. R and A are both correct but R does not causally explain A's description of 31B's purpose.

Value Addition:
• The Ninth Schedule was created precisely because Parliament feared courts would strike down zamindari abolition laws — as they had begun to do before the 1st Amendment.
• IR Coelho's nine-judge bench is one of only three nine-judge benches in recent decades (others: Kesavananda and Property Owners Association 2024).
• Post-IR Coelho, a petitioner challenging a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law must demonstrate Basic Structure violation — not merely FR infringement.

hi.display_text:
कथन (a): संविधान का अनुच्छेद 31B Ninth Schedule में रखे गए कानूनों को भाग III के तहत गारंटीकृत मौलिक अधिकारों के उल्लंघन के आधार पर चुनौती दिए जाने से बचाता है।

कारण (R): सुप्रीम कोर्ट के IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) के निर्णय के बाद, 24 अप्रैल 1973 से पहले Ninth Schedule में डाले गए कानून न्यायिक समीक्षा से पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा का आनंद लेते हैं, जिसमें मौलिक अधिकार उल्लंघन के आधार पर समीक्षा भी शामिल है।

(a) A और R दोनों सही हैं, और R, A की सही व्याख्या है
(b) A और R दोनों सही हैं, लेकिन R, A की सही व्याख्या नहीं है
(c) A सही है लेकिन R गलत है
(d) A गलत है लेकिन R सही है
hi.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प c (A सही है लेकिन R गलत) उन छात्रों को भ्रमित करता है जो मानते हैं कि IR Coelho ने सभी Ninth Schedule कानूनों की समीक्षा योग्यता सुनिश्चित की, जिससे R का पूर्व-1973 पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा के बारे में दावा गलत हो जाता — लेकिन पूर्व-1973 के कानून पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा बनाए रखते हैं, जिससे R सही है।
elimination_logic: चरण 1: क्या कथन (a) तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है? — हाँ। अनुच्छेद 31B उन कानूनों को जो Ninth Schedule में रखे गए हैं, मौलिक अधिकारों के उल्लंघन के आधार पर चुनौती से प्रतिरक्षा प्रदान करता है — यह इसका घोषित कार्य है।

चरण 2: क्या कारण (R) तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है? — हाँ। IR Coelho (2007) के बाद, 24 अप्रैल 1973 से पहले Ninth Schedule में डाले गए कानून पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा बनाए रखते हैं — R IR Coelho के बाद की कानूनी स्थिति के बारे में एक सही और सटीक कथन है।

चरण 3: क्या R, A को कारणात्मक या तार्किक रूप से समझाता है? — आंशिक रूप से। R 31B की प्रतिरक्षा की सीमा (जो IR Coelho के बाद बची) को सही ढंग से वर्णित करता है लेकिन यह पूरी तरह से यह नहीं बताता कि 31B क्यों बनाया गया था (जो कि भूमि सुधार कानूनों को मौलिक अधिकारों की चुनौतियों से बचाना था)। R 31B की वर्तमान सीमा को बताता है न कि इसके मूल तर्क को — A के 31B के उद्देश्य के वर्णन और R के IR Coelho के बाद की सीमा के बीच कारणात्मक संबंध अधूरा है।
A और R दोनों सही हैं, लेकिन R 31B की प्रतिरक्षा की समयगत सीमा को बताता है न कि 31B की सुरक्षात्मक भूमिका को कारणात्मक रूप से समझाता है — विकल्प b।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: स्कोप-एक्सटेंशन ट्रैप इस प्रकार काम करता है कि R इस तरह से बनाया गया है: यह सही ढंग से बताता है कि पूर्व-1973 के Ninth Schedule कानून पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा बनाए रखते हैं लेकिन यह जोड़ता है 'यह प्रतिरक्षा अनुच्छेद 31B का मूल उद्देश्य था।' यह मूल उद्देश्य (सभी Ninth Schedule कानूनों को मौलिक अधिकारों की चुनौती से बचाना) और IR Coelho के बाद बची हुई स्थिति (पूर्व-1973 पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा) को मिला देता है। R IR Coelho के बाद के कानून के बारे में तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है लेकिन यह कारणात्मक रूप से यह नहीं बताता कि अनुच्छेद 31B 1951 में क्यों डाला गया था।
hi.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 31B और Ninth Schedule एक ढाल के रूप में कार्य करते हैं — लेकिन जिसे छह दशकों से अधिक समय में न्यायिक समीक्षा ने पुनः आकार दिया है।

कथन (a) विश्लेषण: अनुच्छेद 31B, जो प्रथम संशोधन (1951) द्वारा डाला गया था, घोषित करता है कि Ninth Schedule में निर्दिष्ट अधिनियम और नियम मौलिक अधिकारों के साथ असंगत होने या उन्हें छीनने या सीमित करने के आधार पर अमान्य नहीं माने जाएंगे। यह 31B की सुरक्षात्मक भूमिका का सही वर्णन है।

कारण (R) विश्लेषण: IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) के बाद, 24 अप्रैल 1973 से पहले Ninth Schedule में डाले गए कानून न्यायिक समीक्षा से पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा बनाए रखते हैं। यह वर्तमान कानूनी स्थिति के बारे में सही कथन है — वामन राव (1981) और IR Coelho (2007) ने मिलकर यह समयगत विभाजन बनाया है।

कारणात्मक संबंध: R तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है लेकिन यह IR Coelho के निर्णय के 31B की सीमा पर प्रभाव का परिणाम बताता है — न कि 31B के डाले जाने के मूल तर्क को। प्रथम संशोधन ने 31B को जमींदारी उन्मूलन कानूनों को सभी मौलिक अधिकार चुनौतियों से बचाने के लिए बनाया था; पूर्व-1973 पूर्ण प्रतिरक्षा IR Coelho के बाद बची हुई स्थिति है। R और A दोनों सही हैं लेकिन R कारणात्मक रूप से A के 31B के उद्देश्य के वर्णन को समझाता नहीं है।

Value Addition:
• Ninth Schedule इसलिए बनाया गया था क्योंकि संसद को डर था कि न्यायालय जमींदारी उन्मूलन कानूनों को रद्द कर देंगे — जैसा कि प्रथम संशोधन से पहले हो रहा था।
• IR Coelho की नौ-न्यायाधीश पीठ हाल के दशकों में केवल तीन नौ-न्यायाधीश पीठों में से एक है (अन्य: Kesavananda और Property Owners Association 2024)।
• IR Coelho के बाद, 1973 के बाद के Ninth Schedule कानून को चुनौती देने वाले याचिकाकर्ता को मौलिक संरचना उल्लंघन दिखाना होगा — केवल मौलिक अधिकार उल्लंघन नहीं।

Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the constitutional and judicial developments listed below?

1. Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras — Supreme Court ruling that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles
2. Twenty-Fifth Constitutional Amendment inserting Article 31C
3. Minerva Mills v. Union of India — Supreme Court striking down DPSP supremacy over Fundamental Rights
4. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation — Supreme Court reading Article 39(a) into Article 21

(a) 1 → 3 → 2 → 4
(b) 1 → 2 → 4 → 3
(c) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
(d) 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
en.strong_distractor: b — Option b places Olga Tellis before Minerva Mills — students who associate both with the 1980s but have not fixed their sequence precisely may accept this order, especially since both deal with expanded Article 21.
elimination_logic: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) is the first event — the earliest DPSP-FR conflict case, predating all others.
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) — twenty years after Champakam; this is the second event.
Minerva Mills v. Union of India was decided in 1980 — after the 25th Amendment; third in sequence.
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation was decided in 1985 — after Minerva Mills; last in sequence. Correct order: Champakam → 25th Amendment → Minerva Mills → Olga Tellis = option c.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the Minerva Mills (1980) / Olga Tellis (1985) pair — both are 1980s Supreme Court cases and students often reverse their order. Additionally, students may misplace the 25th Amendment (1971) as either before or after Minerva Mills without fixing the precise year. The correct sequence requires fixing four events across four decades.
en.final_explanation:
The evolution of the DPSP-Fundamental Rights relationship spans five decades of judicial and legislative action.

Correct sequence:
1. Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951) — First DPSP-FR conflict case; Supreme Court held FRs prevail over DPSPs; directly triggered the 1st Amendment.
2. Twenty-Fifth Amendment inserting Article 31C (1971) — Parliament's attempt to give DPSP Articles 39(b) and (c) a constitutional shield against Articles 14 and 19; represented a partial legislative reversal of Champakam's principle for specific DPSPs.
3. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) — Supreme Court struck down 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C; established the 'balance between FRs and DPSPs is Basic Structure' doctrine.
4. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) — Supreme Court read DPSP Article 39(a) into Article 21 to derive the right to livelihood; demonstrated the judicial technique of DPSP-informed FR expansion.

Wrong options eliminated: Any option placing Minerva Mills after Olga Tellis reverses the 1980/1985 sequence. Any option placing the 25th Amendment before 1951 events is obviously incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The four events represent four distinct phases: judicial (1951), legislative (1971), judicial counter (1980), judicial expansion (1985).
• Each phase represents a different technique of managing the FR-DPSP relationship: conflict resolution, constitutional shielding, balance maintenance, and harmonious expansion.
• Olga Tellis (1985) is sometimes called the 'pavement dwellers case' and is a landmark in socio-economic rights jurisprudence.

shared.concept_anchor: N.M. Thomas — Article 16(d) as facet not exception to 16(a)

en.display_text:
In State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976), the Supreme Court characterised Article 16(d), which provides for reservations in public employment for backward classes, as ________ of Article 16(a) rather than as a departure from it, thereby enabling the implementation of DPSP Article 46 without constitutional conflict.

(a) An exception to the general rule of equality in public employment guaranteed
(b) A facet or positive expression of the principle of equality enshrined
(c) A limitation on the power of Parliament to legislate on matters of public employment
(d) A contradiction within the Constitution that must be resolved by giving preference to the earlier sub-article
en.strong_distractor: a — Option a ('an exception to the general rule of equality') is the classic pre-N.M. Thomas characterisation of Article 16(d) — students who have not specifically studied this case will naturally choose this formulation, which was the prevailing understanding before the judgment.
elimination_logic: The N.M. Thomas (1976) case specifically addressed whether Article 16(d) is an exception to Article 16(a) or something else.
The Court held Article 16(d) is NOT an exception but a 'facet' or 'application' of Article 16(a) — treating equality in substance rather than form.
Eliminate option a — 'exception' is the pre-N.M. Thomas characterisation that the judgment specifically rejected.
Eliminate options c and d — neither 'limitation' nor 'contradiction' reflects the Court's positive characterisation; option b ('facet') is the precise term used.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a ('an exception to Article 16(a)') was the legal orthodoxy before N.M. Thomas (1976) and remains the intuitive understanding for most students. The trap exploits this pre-existing intuition: students who have not specifically studied the N.M. Thomas holding will confidently select 'exception' because Article 16(d) does carve out a special category for backward classes, making it appear exception-like on the surface. The judgment's profound innovation was to recast this as a positive expression of equality rather than a departure from it.
en.final_explanation:
N.M. Thomas (1976) reframed the constitutional understanding of the relationship between Article 16(a) (equality of opportunity in public employment) and Article 16(d) (reservations for backward classes).

• Option (a): Incorrect. 'An exception to the general rule of equality' was the pre-N.M. Thomas orthodox view — the judgment specifically rejected this characterisation.
• Option (b): Correct. The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas held that Article 16(d) is a 'facet' of Article 16(a) — it is not a departure from equality but an expression of substantive equality. Treating backward classes specially IS treating them equally in a material sense.
• Option (c): Incorrect. 'A limitation on the power of Parliament' mischaracterises Article 16(d) — it is an enabling provision (States MAY make reservations), not a limitation on Parliament.
• Option (d): Incorrect. 'A contradiction within the Constitution' is never an acceptable judicial characterisation of a constitutional provision.

Value Addition:
• N.M. Thomas (1976) pre-dates Indra Sawhney (Mandal Commission case, 1992) and laid the doctrinal groundwork for the facet/expression-of-equality view of reservations.
• The case established that implementing DPSP Article 46 (welfare of SCs/STs) through reservations harmonises with, rather than conflicts with, Article 16.
• Post-N.M. Thomas, Article 16(d) is understood as enabling backward class representation — a positive constitutional goal, not an exception to equality.

(a) सार्वजनिक रोजगार में समानता के सामान्य नियम का एक अपवाद
(b) समानता के सिद्धांत की एक पहलू या सकारात्मक अभिव्यक्ति
(c) सार्वजनिक रोजगार के मामलों में संसद के विधायी अधिकार पर एक सीमा

hi.strong_distractor: a — विकल्प a ('समानता के सामान्य नियम से एक अपवाद') अनुच्छेद 16(d) के लिए N.M. Thomas से पहले की पारंपरिक व्याख्या है — जो छात्र इस मामले का विशेष अध्ययन नहीं करते हैं, वे स्वाभाविक रूप से इस व्याख्या को चुनेंगे, जो निर्णय से पहले प्रचलित समझ थी।

विकल्प a को हटाएं — 'अपवाद' वह पूर्व-N.M. Thomas व्याख्या है जिसे निर्णय ने स्पष्ट रूप से खारिज किया।
विकल्प c और d को हटाएं — न तो 'सीमा' और न ही 'विरोधाभास' अदालत की सकारात्मक व्याख्या को दर्शाते हैं; विकल्प b ('पहलू') सटीक शब्द है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: विकल्प a ('अनुच्छेद 16(a) का अपवाद') N.M. Thomas (1976) से पहले की कानूनी मान्यता थी और अधिकांश छात्रों के लिए सहज समझ बनी हुई है। यह जाल इस पूर्व-विद्यमान सहज ज्ञान पर आधारित है: जो छात्र N.M. Thomas के निर्णय का विशेष अध्ययन नहीं करते, वे 'अपवाद' को चुनेंगे क्योंकि अनुच्छेद 16(d) पिछड़ी जातियों के लिए विशेष वर्ग बनाता है, जो सतह पर अपवाद जैसा प्रतीत होता है। निर्णय की गहन नवीनता इसे समानता से विचलन के बजाय समानता की सकारात्मक अभिव्यक्ति के रूप में पुनः प्रस्तुत करना था।
hi.final_explanation:
N.M. Thomas (1976) ने अनुच्छेद 16(a) (सार्वजनिक रोजगार में अवसर की समानता) और अनुच्छेद 16(d) (पिछड़ी जातियों के लिए आरक्षण) के बीच संबंध की संवैधानिक समझ को पुनः परिभाषित किया।

• विकल्प (a): गलत। 'समानता के सामान्य नियम का अपवाद' पूर्व-N.M. Thomas की पारंपरिक दृष्टि थी — इस व्याख्या को निर्णय ने स्पष्ट रूप से खारिज किया।
• विकल्प (b): सही। केरल राज्य बनाम N.M. Thomas में सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने कहा कि अनुच्छेद 16(d) अनुच्छेद 16(a) का 'पहलू' है — यह समानता से विचलन नहीं बल्कि सार्थक समानता की अभिव्यक्ति है। पिछड़ी जातियों के लिए विशेष व्यवहार करना वास्तव में उन्हें सामग्रीगत रूप से समानता देना है।
• विकल्प (c): गलत। 'संसद के विधायी अधिकार पर एक सीमा' अनुच्छेद 16(d) की गलत व्याख्या है — यह एक सक्षम करने वाला प्रावधान है (राज्य आरक्षण कर सकते हैं), संसद पर कोई सीमा नहीं।
• विकल्प (d): गलत। 'संविधान के भीतर एक विरोधाभास' कभी भी संवैधानिक प्रावधान की स्वीकार्य न्यायिक व्याख्या नहीं हो सकती।

Value Addition:
• N.M. Thomas (1976) इंद्रा साहनी (मंडल आयोग मामला, 1992) से पहले का मामला है और आरक्षण के पहलू/समानता की अभिव्यक्ति के दृष्टिकोण के लिए सैद्धांतिक आधार स्थापित करता है।
• इस मामले ने यह स्थापित किया कि DPSP अनुच्छेद 46 (अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति के कल्याण) को आरक्षण के माध्यम से लागू करना अनुच्छेद 16 के साथ विरोधाभासी नहीं बल्कि सामंजस्यपूर्ण है।
• N.M. Thomas के बाद, अनुच्छेद 16(d) को पिछड़ी जातियों के प्रतिनिधित्व को सक्षम करने वाला एक सकारात्मक संवैधानिक लक्ष्य माना जाता है, न कि समानता का अपवाद।

en.display_text:
Which of the following pairs relating to Article 31C of the Constitution is correctly matched in its current operative form?

(a) Article 31C — Protects laws giving effect to all Directive Principles of State Policy from challenge under Articles 14 and 19
(b) Article 31C — Inserted by the Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment (1976) to shield Directive Principles-implementing laws from judicial review
(c) Article 31C — Protects laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, as upheld by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980)
(d) Article 31C — Situated in Part IV of the Constitution as an integral part of the Directive Principles of State Policy
en.strong_distractor: a — Option a pairs Article 31C with 'laws implementing all Directive Principles' — the trap exploits the 42nd Amendment's attempted expansion (which was struck down), making students who recall 'the 42nd Amendment tried to extend 31C' incorrectly believe it succeeded.
elimination_logic: Post-Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) — not all DPSPs.
Eliminate option a — 'all Directive Principles' was the 42nd Amendment's expansion, struck down in Minerva Mills; this pairing is incorrect.
Eliminate option b — Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), not the 42nd Amendment (1976).

Eliminate option d — Article 31C is in Part III (as a modification to Article 31), not Part IV; option c correctly pairs Article 31C with its current operative scope (protecting 39(b) and (c) laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenge).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a exploits a conflation trap: the 42nd Amendment DID attempt to expand Article 31C to all DPSPs — and students who recall this expansion may assume it succeeded or that 'Article 31C = all DPSPs' is the current position. The Minerva Mills reversal is the key fact that defeats this assumption. Option b additionally conflates the inserting amendment (25th) with the expanding amendment (42nd), adding a temporal-swap layer.
en.final_explanation:
Article 31C's current operative scope is one of the most frequently examined facts in DPSP questions — and the conflation with the 42nd Amendment's failed expansion is a persistent source of errors.

• Option (a): Incorrectly paired. Article 31C does NOT protect laws implementing all Directive Principles — this was the 42nd Amendment's expansion, struck down in Minerva Mills (1980). The current scope is limited to Articles 39(b) and (c) only.
• Option (b): Incorrectly paired. Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment (1971), not the Forty-Second Amendment. The 42nd Amendment tried to expand its scope, not create it.
• Option (c): Correctly paired. Article 31C, in its post-Minerva Mills operative form, protects laws specifically giving effect to Articles 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 — this is the accurate and current constitutional position.
• Option (d): Incorrectly paired. Article 31C is not located in Part IV (DPSPs); it is inserted in Part III as a qualification to the operation of Fundamental Rights — placed after Article 31A and 31B.

Value Addition:
• Articles 39(b) and (c) are the ONLY DPSPs that enjoy Article 31C protection — uniquely privileged among all 20+ DPSPs.
• Article 31C's protection against Article 19 means laws implementing 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged on grounds of unreasonable restrictions on property, trade, or profession rights.
• The 2024 Property Owners Association case reconsidered the scope of 'material resources' under 39(b) — showing this provision remains constitutionally live.

shared.concept_anchor: Three-case arc — Champakam to Kesavananda to Minerva Mills on FR-DPSP

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements about the three landmark Supreme Court decisions that shaped the constitutional relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles:

1. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) established that in case of direct conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles — and this ruling was the only Supreme Court judgment to be immediately 'overcome' by a constitutional amendment that added a new Fundamental Rights clause (Article 15(d)).
2. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights is unrestricted as long as the amendment serves the objectives set out in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
3. Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the Basic Structure, meaning Parliament cannot tip the constitutional scales entirely in favour of either Part III or Part IV.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) established that in case of direct conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles — and this ruling was the only Supreme Court judgment to be immediately 'overcome' by a constitutional amendment that added a new Fundamental Rights clause (Article 15(d)).
statement_analysis.reason: Champakam is correctly described as the first FR-DPSP conflict case; and Article 15(d) added by the 1st Amendment is correctly characterised as a constitutional amendment responding to a Supreme Court judgment by adding to Part III itself — this is historically unique.

statement_analysis.statement: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights is unrestricted as long as the amendment serves the objectives set out in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
statement_analysis.reason: Kesavananda held the opposite — Parliament's amending power is LIMITED by the Basic Structure doctrine; amendments cannot destroy essential features even if intended to implement DPSPs. The case overruled the unlimited amendment power view from Golak Nath was being contested.

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the Basic Structure, meaning Parliament cannot tip the constitutional scales entirely in favour of either Part III or Part IV.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise holding of Minerva Mills — the harmony between the two sets of provisions is constitutionally mandated and cannot be destroyed by any amendment, making neither part absolutely dominant.

en.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who know all three cases are major FR-DPSP milestones and accept Statement 2's description without noting that Kesavananda established LIMITS on amending power — not unlimited power with a DPSP-purpose qualification.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Champakam is correctly described, and Article 15(d) being added to Part III (not Part IV) in response to a Part III ruling is indeed historically unique; Statement 1 is correct.

Identify the fundamental error in Statement 2 — Kesavananda held Parliament's amending power has LIMITS (Basic Structure); it did NOT hold that DPSP-motivated amendments are unrestricted; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — Minerva Mills' holding that the FR-DPSP balance is Basic Structure is precisely stated; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option a (1 and 3 only).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: Kesavananda IS associated with DPSPs (it upheld the first part of Article 31C), and students may construct a connection between DPSP-motivated amendments and parliamentary power. The statement sounds reasonable — 'Parliament can amend FRs if it's for DPSPs' — but this is exactly the position Minerva Mills (1980) rejected, building on Kesavananda's Basic Structure constraint.
en.final_explanation:
The three-case arc from Champakam (1951) to Kesavananda (1973) to Minerva Mills (1980) represents the complete judicial evolution of the FR-DPSP relationship.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Champakam established FR supremacy over DPSPs in 1951. Parliament responded with the 1st Amendment adding Article 15(d) — a new clause within Part III (Fundamental Rights) itself, not a DPSP. This is unique: a judgment on Part III was overcome by adding to Part III rather than amending Part IV.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Kesavananda established LIMITS on Parliament's amending power through Basic Structure — it did not grant Parliament unlimited amending authority for DPSP purposes. The Basic Structure doctrine means some features cannot be destroyed even by DPSP-motivated amendments.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Minerva Mills synthesised Kesavananda's Basic Structure constraint with the DPSP framework by holding that the balance between Part III and Part IV is itself Basic Structure — neither can be made absolutely superior to the other.

Value Addition:
• The 1st Amendment's addition of Article 15(d) to Part III is the only instance of a constitutional amendment 'defeating' a Supreme Court judgment by expanding the very Part the Court had applied.
• Kesavananda's thirteen-judge bench included Chief Justice Sikri — retired the same day the judgment was delivered, which was also his last day in office.
• Minerva Mills (1980) also struck down Section 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which had made Parliament's amending power immune from judicial review — doubly reasserting Basic Structure.

hi.final_explanation:
Champakam (1951) से Kesavananda (1973) से Minerva Mills (1980) तक तीन-मामलों की श्रृंखला FR-DPSP संबंध के न्यायिक विकास का पूर्ण प्रतिनिधित्व करती है।

• कथन 1 — सही: Champakam ने 1951 में FR की DPSPs पर श्रेष्ठता स्थापित की। संसद ने 1st Amendment के साथ अनुच्छेद 15(d) जोड़ा — जो पार्ट III (मौलिक अधिकार) के भीतर एक नया प्रावधान है, DPSP नहीं। यह अद्वितीय है: पार्ट III पर निर्णय को पार्ट III में जोड़कर पार किया गया, न कि पार्ट IV में संशोधन करके।
• कथन 2 — गलत: Kesavananda ने Basic Structure के माध्यम से संसद की संशोधन शक्ति पर सीमाएँ स्थापित कीं — उसने संसद को DPSP उद्देश्यों के लिए असीमित संशोधन अधिकार नहीं दिया। Basic Structure सिद्धांत का अर्थ है कि कुछ विशेषताएँ DPSP-प्रेरित संशोधनों से भी नष्ट नहीं की जा सकतीं।
• कथन 3 — सही: Minerva Mills ने Kesavananda के Basic Structure प्रतिबंध को DPSP ढांचे के साथ जोड़ा और कहा कि पार्ट III और पार्ट IV के बीच संतुलन स्वयं Basic Structure है — कोई भी पक्ष पूर्णतः प्रभुत्वशाली नहीं हो सकता।

Value Addition:
• 1st Amendment द्वारा अनुच्छेद 15(d) का पार्ट III में जोड़ना एकमात्र ऐसा संवैधानिक संशोधन है जिसने सुप्रीम कोर्ट के निर्णय को उसी पार्ट को बढ़ाकर 'पराजित' किया।
• Kesavananda के तेरह-न्यायाधीशों के बेंच में मुख्य न्यायाधीश सिकरी शामिल थे — जो उसी दिन सेवानिवृत्त हुए जब यह निर्णय दिया गया, जो उनका अंतिम कार्यदिवस भी था।
• Minerva Mills (1980) ने 42वें संशोधन की धारा 55 को भी रद्द किया, जिसने संसद की संशोधन शक्ति को न्यायिक समीक्षा से मुक्त कर दिया था — जिससे Basic Structure सिद्धांत की पुनः पुष्टि हुई।

elimination_logic: The 42nd Amendment is uniquely known for adding three new DPSPs AND having its supremacy provisions struck down — no other amendment matches this dual profile.

The 86th Amendment AMENDED an existing DPSP (Article 45) — narrowing its scope and simultaneously creating Article 21A as a new FR; the amendment changed the content of an existing DPSP rather than adding a new one.
The 97th Amendment added a new DPSP (Article 43B) AND expanded an existing FR (Article 19(a)(c)) AND was partially struck down in 2021 — this three-feature profile matches List II item 4.
The 25th Amendment inserted Article 31C alone — no new DPSP was added; it was a shield provision. This matches List II item 1. Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 = option b.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between the 86th and 97th Amendments is the primary trap: both involved simultaneous changes to FRs and DPSPs. The distinction is that the 86th Amendment AMENDED (narrowed) an existing DPSP (Article 45), while the 97th Amendment ADDED a new DPSP (Article 43B). Additionally, only the 97th Amendment was partially struck down. Students who blur these distinctions will misplace the amendments in List II.
en.final_explanation:
Distinguishing the constitutional features of each major DPSP-related amendment requires precise knowledge of what each amendment added, changed, and what judicial fate it met.

Correct pairings:
• A (42nd Amendment, 1976) — 3: Added three new DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A) — the maximum added by any single amendment — while simultaneously attempting (unsuccessfully) to give DPSPs supremacy over FRs.
• B (25th Amendment, 1971) — 1: Inserted Article 31C alone — a shield for laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c); did not add any new DPSP article to Part IV.
• C (86th Amendment, 2002) — 2: Amended the existing Article 45 (DPSP) to cover only under-6 children while inserting Article 21A (FR) for children aged 6–14 — uniquely amended an existing DPSP's scope.
• D (97th Amendment, 2011) — 4: Added Article 43B (new DPSP) + expanded Article 19(a)(c) (FR) + was partially struck down in Rajendra N. Shah (2021) for state cooperative society provisions.

Trap pairings: C–4 and D–2 are the expected swaps — students confuse which amendment involved partial judicial invalidation and which amended an existing DPSP.

Value Addition:
• No other constitutional amendment has combined adding a new FR, amending an existing DPSP, and adding a new Fundamental Duty in a single act — the 86th Amendment did all three.
• The 97th Amendment's partial invalidation in 2021 is the most recent major DPSP-related judicial decision.
• The 25th Amendment's Article 31C was judicially modified twice — first by Kesavananda (1973) and then indirectly by Minerva Mills (1980).

hi.final_explanation:
प्रत्येक प्रमुख DPSP-संबंधित संशोधन की संवैधानिक विशेषताओं को अलग करने के लिए यह जानना आवश्यक है कि प्रत्येक संशोधन ने क्या जोड़ा, बदला और उसका न्यायिक परिणाम क्या रहा।

सही जोड़े:
• A (42वां संशोधन, 1976) — 3: तीन नए DPSP (39A, 43A, 48A) जोड़े — किसी एक संशोधन द्वारा जोड़े गए अधिकतम — साथ ही DPSP को मौलिक अधिकारों पर सर्वोच्चता देने का प्रयास (असफल)।
• B (25वां संशोधन, 1971) — 1: केवल अनुच्छेद 31C डाला — अनुच्छेद 39(b) और (c) को लागू करने वाले कानूनों के लिए सुरक्षा; Part IV में कोई नया DPSP अनुच्छेद नहीं जोड़ा।
• C (86वां संशोधन, 2002) — 2: मौजूदा अनुच्छेद 45 (DPSP) को केवल 6 वर्ष से कम उम्र के बच्चों तक सीमित किया और साथ ही 6-14 वर्ष के बच्चों के लिए अनुच्छेद 21A (मौलिक अधिकार) जोड़ा — एक मौजूदा DPSP के दायरे में अनूठा संशोधन।
• D (97वां संशोधन, 2011) — 4: नया DPSP (अनुच्छेद 43B) जोड़ा + मौलिक अधिकार (अनुच्छेद 19(a)(c)) का विस्तार किया + राज्य सहकारी सोसाइटी प्रावधानों के लिए आंशिक रूप से निरस्त किया गया (राजेंद्र एन. शाह, 2021)।

shared.concept_anchor: DPSP enforcement technique — reading into FRs not direct enforcement

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements about the judicial approach to Directive Principles of State Policy in three landmark cases:

1. In Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993), the Supreme Court held that because Article 45 (DPSP) is non-justiciable, the right to education cannot be recognised as enforceable in any form prior to a constitutional amendment.
2. N.M. Thomas (1976) demonstrated that DPSPs can inform the interpretation of Fundamental Rights, enabling a court to read a Fundamental Right provision more broadly to accommodate DPSP objectives.
3. The judicial technique of reading DPSPs into Article 21 to expand the right to life was first employed in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), using Article 39(a) to include the right to livelihood within Article 21.

Which of the above statements is/are NOT correct?

(a) 2 and 3 only
(b) 2 only
(c) 3 only
(d) 1 only

statement_analysis.statement: In Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993), the Supreme Court held that because Article 45 (DPSP) is non-justiciable, the right to education cannot be recognised as enforceable in any form prior to a constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Unnikrishnan (1993) held exactly the opposite — the Court derived the right to education for under-14 children as a Fundamental Right by reading Article 45 INTO Article 21, creating an enforceable right without a constitutional amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: N.M. Thomas (1976) demonstrated that DPSPs can inform the INTERPRETATION of Fundamental Rights, enabling a court to read a Fundamental Right provision more broadly to accommodate DPSP objectives.
statement_analysis.reason: N.M. Thomas used DPSP Article 46 to inform the interpretation of Article 16(a) — holding that substantive equality (giving effect to 46) is consistent with Article 16(a)'s equality mandate, demonstrating the interpretive role of DPSPs.

statement_analysis.statement: The judicial technique of reading DPSPs into Article 21 to expand the right to life was first employed in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), using Article 39(a) to include the right to livelihood within Article 21.
statement_analysis.reason: Olga Tellis (1985) is indeed credited with pioneering the Article 39(a)+Article 21 reading to derive the right to livelihood — it is among the earliest applications of this technique to a socio-economic DPSP.

en.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Statement 2 only incorrect) is the strong distractor because Statement 2 correctly describes N.M. Thomas and students who know this case will confidently mark Statement 2 as correct — but they must also identify Statement 1 as incorrect (it reverses the Unnikrishnan holding).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 contains a reversed-causation error — Unnikrishnan did NOT hold that DPSP non-justiciability prevents any right derivation; it did the opposite, deriving the right to education via Article 21+45.
Statement 2 is correct — N.M. Thomas is precisely about DPSPs informing FR interpretation.
Statement 3 is correct — Olga Tellis pioneered the Article 39(a)+21 technique for the right to livelihood.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect → option d (Statement 1 only NOT correct).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a reversed-causation trap: the statement implies that because DPSPs are non-justiciable, a court must wait for a constitutional amendment before recognising any DPSP-grounded right. But Unnikrishnan (1993) did the reverse — it used the non-justiciable DPSP (Article 45) as interpretive material to EXPAND a Fundamental Right (Article 21), creating an enforceable right without any constitutional amendment. This reversal of the judicial technique is the core error.
en.final_explanation:
The three cases in this question represent the sophisticated judicial toolkit for making DPSP objectives practically enforceable without amending the Constitution.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993) held that the right to education for children up to 14 years IS a Fundamental Right — derived from Article 21 read with Article 45 (DPSP). The Court did NOT hold that non-justiciability of 45 bars any enforceable right before a formal amendment. The statement completely reverses the judgment's holding.
• Statement 2 — Correct: N.M. Thomas demonstrated the interpretive role of DPSPs — Article 46 (welfare of SCs/STs) was used to read Article 16(a)'s equality mandate substantively, enabling reservations to coexist with equality rather than conflict with it.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Olga Tellis (1985) is the landmark case for the Article 39(a)+Article 21 technique. By holding that life without means of livelihood is not 'life' in the constitutional sense, the Court enforcibly embedded a DPSP objective within a Fundamental Right.

Only Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Value Addition:
• The three judicial techniques — reading DPSPs into FRs (Olga Tellis), using DPSPs to interpret FRs (N.M. Thomas), and DPSP+Article 21 derivation (Unnikrishnan) — together constitute India's 'social rights jurisprudence.'
• Post-86th Amendment (2002), the Unnikrishnan judicial derivation was formalised as Article 21A — showing how judicial creativity eventually becomes constitutional text.
• The non-justiciability of DPSPs (Article 37) is therefore not an absolute barrier — it prevents direct enforcement through writs but not indirect enforcement via FR interpretation.

hi.display_text:
तीन मील के पत्थर मामलों में राज्य नीति के निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांतों (DPSP) के न्यायिक दृष्टिकोण के बारे में निम्नलिखित कथनों पर विचार करें:

1. Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993) में, सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने कहा कि क्योंकि अनुच्छेद 45 (DPSP) न्यायिक रूप से लागू नहीं है, इसलिए शिक्षा का अधिकार किसी भी रूप में संवैधानिक संशोधन से पहले लागू नहीं किया जा सकता।
2. N.M. Thomas (1976) ने यह दिखाया कि DPSP मौलिक अधिकारों की व्याख्या को सूचित कर सकते हैं, जिससे न्यायालय मौलिक अधिकार के प्रावधान को DPSP उद्देश्यों के अनुरूप व्यापक रूप से पढ़ सकता है।
3. DPSP को अनुच्छेद 21 में पढ़कर जीवन के अधिकार का विस्तार करने की न्यायिक तकनीक का पहला उपयोग Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) में किया गया, जिसमें अनुच्छेद 39(a) का उपयोग कर जीविकोपार्जन के अधिकार को अनुच्छेद 21 में शामिल किया गया।

उपरोक्त में से कौन-सा/से कथन सही नहीं है/हैं?

(a) केवल 2 और 3
(b) केवल 2

en.display_text:
A State legislature enacts a law that mandates compulsory representation of workers on the board of management of large private sector enterprises, implementing a Directive Principle of State Policy on workers' participation in industrial management. A business association challenges the law before a constitutional court, arguing that it violates their right to carry on business freely under Article 19. The law does not involve distribution of material resources and is not specifically covered under Article 31C. Which of the following most accurately describes the approach a constitutional court would adopt, consistent with the current constitutional position?

(a) The court must strike down the law because Article 19 is a Fundamental Right and automatically prevails over any Directive Principle that conflicts with it, in accordance with the principle established in Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
(b) The court must attempt to harmoniously construct the Directive Principle and the Fundamental Right, recognising that neither Part III nor Part IV is absolutely superior, and uphold the law if it imposes only a reasonable restriction on Article 19 in furtherance of a public interest objective
(c) The court must uphold the law because Article 31C protects any legislation that implements a Directive Principle of State Policy from challenge under Article 19, regardless of which specific DPSP is involved
(d) The court must uphold the law because the Forty-Second Amendment gave Directive Principles supremacy over Fundamental Rights, making legislative action implementing DPSPs immune from Article 19 challenge
en.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Article 31C shields any DPSP law from any FR challenge) is the conflation distractor — it blends the 42nd Amendment's invalidated expansion with the surviving Article 31C, making students who recall 'Article 31C protects DPSP laws' choose this broad (and incorrect) formulation.
elimination_logic: The scenario presents a labour welfare law (implementing DPSP) challenged under Article 19 — the court must navigate FR-DPSP tension.
The governing principle after Minerva Mills (1980) is harmonious construction — courts should read FRs and DPSPs together rather than making one absolutely superior.
Eliminate option a (Article 19 automatically prevails) — this is the pre-42nd Amendment Champakam orthodoxy, which Minerva Mills qualified by establishing the balance as Basic Structure.
Eliminate option c (Article 31C shields any DPSP law) — Article 31C protects only 39(b) and (c) laws; the scenario's DPSP may not be 39(b)/(c).
Eliminate option d (DPSPs prevail as per 42nd Amendment) — this provision was struck down in Minerva Mills.
Option b correctly identifies harmonious construction as the Minerva Mills doctrine applicable to FR-DPSP tension.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c conflates the surviving and invalidated parts of Article 31C: it presents 'Article 31C shields any DPSP-implementing law' as if the 42nd Amendment's expansion survived. Students who know Article 31C is relevant to DPSP-FR conflicts may accept this broad formulation without recalling that Minerva Mills confined the shield to 39(b) and (c) only. The scenario's law may implement a different DPSP, making option c inapplicable.
en.final_explanation:
When a law implementing a Directive Principle is challenged on grounds of violating a Fundamental Right, the governing judicial doctrine — post Minerva Mills (1980) — is harmonious construction.

Applicable principle: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the Basic Structure. Courts are therefore required to read the two sets of provisions harmoniously — neither should be made absolutely superior. This is the doctrine of harmonious construction applied at the constitutional level.

Scenario mapping: A law implementing a DPSP (labour welfare) challenged under Article 19 (freedom to carry on trade or business) should be examined for whether a harmonious reading of both provisions is possible — whether the restriction on Article 19 is reasonable in light of DPSP objectives, rather than automatically invalidating the law or automatically upholding it.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Article 19 does not automatically prevail — that was Champakam's (1951) pre-42nd Amendment position, later qualified by Minerva Mills.
• Option (b): Correct. Harmonious construction — reading FRs and DPSPs together to give effect to both where possible — is the Minerva Mills doctrine.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14 and 19. It does not shield all DPSP laws from all FR challenges.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The 42nd Amendment's DPSP supremacy provision was struck down in Minerva Mills — DPSPs do not automatically prevail over FRs.

Value Addition:
• Harmonious construction is the 'preferred reading' in constitutional interpretation — courts avoid conflict between constitutional provisions by reading them together.
• The Minerva Mills balance principle is now the bedrock doctrine: neither FRs nor DPSPs can be made absolute at the other's expense.
• Only if harmonious construction is impossible — genuine irreconcilable conflict — would a court invoke the residual FR precedence from pre-Minerva Mills doctrine.

hi.upsc_trap_explanation: विकल्प (c) अनुच्छेद 31C के जीवित और रद्द किए गए भागों को मिलाता है: यह 'अनुच्छेद 31C किसी भी DPSP-लागू कानून को बचाता है' प्रस्तुत करता है जैसे कि 42वें संशोधन का विस्तार जीवित है। जो छात्र जानते हैं कि अनुच्छेद 31C DPSP-मौलिक अधिकार संघर्षों से संबंधित है, वे इस व्यापक व्याख्या को स्वीकार कर सकते हैं बिना यह याद किए कि Minerva Mills ने सुरक्षा को केवल 39(b) और (c) तक सीमित किया है। परिदृश्य का कानून संभवतः एक अलग DPSP लागू करता है, जिससे विकल्प (c) लागू नहीं होता।
hi.final_explanation:
जब कोई कानून जो एक निर्देशात्मक राज्य नीति सिद्धांत (DPSP) को लागू करता है, मौलिक अधिकार के उल्लंघन के आधार पर चुनौती दी जाती है, तो Minerva Mills (1980) के बाद का न्यायिक सिद्धांत है सामंजस्यपूर्ण व्याख्या।

लागू सिद्धांत: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) में, सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने कहा कि मौलिक अधिकार और निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांतों के बीच संतुलन स्वयं Basic Structure का हिस्सा है। अतः अदालतों को दोनों प्रावधानों को सामंजस्यपूर्ण रूप से पढ़ना चाहिए — किसी एक को पूर्णतः श्रेष्ठ नहीं बनाना चाहिए। यह संवैधानिक स्तर पर लागू सामंजस्यपूर्ण व्याख्या का सिद्धांत है।

परिदृश्य का मिलान: एक DPSP (श्रम कल्याण) लागू करने वाला कानून जिसे अनुच्छेद 19 (व्यापार या व्यवसाय करने की स्वतंत्रता) के तहत चुनौती दी गई है, यह जांचा जाना चाहिए कि क्या दोनों प्रावधानों की सामंजस्यपूर्ण व्याख्या संभव है — क्या अनुच्छेद 19 पर प्रतिबंध DPSP के उद्देश्यों के प्रकाश में उचित है, न कि कानून को स्वतः अमान्य या स्वतः मान्य करना।

• विकल्प (a): गलत। अनुच्छेद 19 स्वतः सर्वोच्च नहीं है — यह Champakam (1951) का 42वें संशोधन से पहले का दृष्टिकोण था, जिसे बाद में Minerva Mills ने संशोधित किया।
• विकल्प (b): सही। सामंजस्यपूर्ण व्याख्या — मौलिक अधिकार और DPSP को एक साथ पढ़ना ताकि दोनों का प्रभाव हो — Minerva Mills का सिद्धांत है।
• विकल्प (c): गलत। अनुच्छेद 31C केवल 39(b) और (c) के कानूनों को अनुच्छेद 14 और 19 के तहत बचाता है। यह सभी DPSP कानूनों को सभी मौलिक अधिकार चुनौतियों से नहीं बचाता।
• विकल्प (d): गलत। 42वें संशोधन का DPSP सर्वोच्चता प्रावधान Minerva Mills में रद्द कर दिया गया — DPSP स्वतः मौलिक अधिकारों पर सर्वोच्च नहीं होते।

Value Addition:
• सामंजस्यपूर्ण व्याख्या संवैधानिक व्याख्या में 'प्राथमिक पठन' है — अदालतें संवैधानिक प्रावधानों के बीच संघर्ष से बचने के लिए उन्हें एक साथ पढ़ती हैं।
• Minerva Mills का संतुलन सिद्धांत अब आधारभूत सिद्धांत है: न तो मौलिक अधिकार न ही DPSP को दूसरे की कीमत पर पूर्णतः श्रेष्ठ बनाया जा सकता है।
• केवल जब सामंजस्यपूर्ण व्याख्या असंभव हो — वास्तविक असंगत संघर्ष — तब अदालत पूर्व-Minerva Mills सिद्धांत के अनुसार मौलिक अधिकार की प्राथमिकता लागू करेगी।
